Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning
Ensemble Techniques and Model Tuning
Visa Approval Facilitation

Problem Statement¶

Context¶

Business communities in the United States are facing high demand for human resources, but one of the constant challenges is identifying and attracting the right talent, which is perhaps the most important element in remaining competitive. Companies in the United States look for hard-working, talented, and qualified individuals both locally as well as abroad.

The Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) of the US permits foreign workers to come to the United States to work on either a temporary or permanent basis. The act also protects US workers against adverse impacts on their wages or working conditions by ensuring US employers' compliance with statutory requirements when they hire foreign workers to fill workforce shortages. The immigration programs are administered by the Office of Foreign Labor Certification (OFLC).

OFLC processes job certification applications for employers seeking to bring foreign workers into the United States and grants certifications in those cases where employers can demonstrate that there are not sufficient US workers available to perform the work at wages that meet or exceed the wage paid for the occupation in the area of intended employment.

Objective¶

In FY 2016, the OFLC processed 775,979 employer applications for 1,699,957 positions for temporary and permanent labor certifications. This was a nine percent increase in the overall number of processed applications from the previous year. The process of reviewing every case is becoming a tedious task as the number of applicants is increasing every year.

The increasing number of applicants every year calls for a Machine Learning based solution that can help in shortlisting the candidates having higher chances of VISA approval. OFLC has hired the firm EasyVisa for data-driven solutions. You as a data scientist at EasyVisa have to analyze the data provided and, with the help of a classification model:

  • Facilitate the process of visa approvals.
  • Recommend a suitable profile for the applicants for whom the visa should be certified or denied based on the drivers that significantly influence the case status.

Data Description¶

The data contains the different attributes of employee and the employer. The detailed data dictionary is given below.

  • case_id: ID of each visa application
  • continent: Information of continent the employee
  • education_of_employee: Information of education of the employee
  • has_job_experience: Does the employee has any job experience? Y= Yes; N = No
  • requires_job_training: Does the employee require any job training? Y = Yes; N = No
  • no_of_employees: Number of employees in the employer's company
  • yr_of_estab: Year in which the employer's company was established
  • region_of_employment: Information of foreign worker's intended region of employment in the US.
  • prevailing_wage: Average wage paid to similarly employed workers in a specific occupation in the area of intended employment. The purpose of the prevailing wage is to ensure that the foreign worker is not underpaid compared to other workers offering the same or similar service in the same area of employment.
  • unit_of_wage: Unit of prevailing wage. Values include Hourly, Weekly, Monthly, and Yearly.
  • full_time_position: Is the position of work full-time? Y = Full Time Position; N = Part Time Position
  • case_status: Flag indicating if the Visa was certified or denied

Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)¶

  • EDA is an important part of any project involving data.
  • It is important to investigate and understand the data better before building a model with it.
  • A few questions have been mentioned below which will help you approach the analysis in the right manner and generate insights from the data.
  • A thorough analysis of the data, in addition to the questions mentioned below, should be done.

Leading Questions

What is the distribution of visa case statuses (certified vs. denied)?

  1. What is the distribution of visa case statuses (certified vs. denied)?
  2. How does the education level of employees impact visa approval rates?
  3. Is there a significant difference in visa approval rates between employees with and without prior job experience?
  4. How does the prevailing wage affect visa approval? Do higher wages lead to higher chances of approval?
  5. Do certain regions in the US have higher visa approval rates compared to others?
  6. How does the number of employees in a company influence visa approval? Do larger companies have a higher approval rate?
  7. Are visa approval rates different across various continents of employees? Which continent has the highest and lowest approval rates?

# function to create labeled barplots


def labeled_barplot(data, feature, perc=False, n=None):
    """
    Barplot with percentage at the top

    data: dataframe
    feature: dataframe column
    perc: whether to display percentages instead of count (default is False)
    n: displays the top n category levels (default is None, i.e., display all levels)
    """

    total = len(data[feature])  # length of the column
    count = data[feature].nunique()
    if n is None:
        plt.figure(figsize=(count + 1, 5))
    else:
        plt.figure(figsize=(n + 1, 5))

    plt.xticks(rotation=90, fontsize=15)
    ax = sns.countplot(
        data=data,
        x=feature,
        palette="Paired",
        order=data[feature].value_counts().index[:n].sort_values(),
    )

    for p in ax.patches:
        if perc == True:
            label = "{:.1f}%".format(
                100 * p.get_height() / total
            )  # percentage of each class of the category
        else:
            label = p.get_height()  # count of each level of the category

        x = p.get_x() + p.get_width() / 2  # width of the plot
        y = p.get_height()  # height of the plot

        ax.annotate(
            label,
            (x, y),
            ha="center",
            va="center",
            size=12,
            xytext=(0, 5),
            textcoords="offset points",
        )  # annotate the percentage

    plt.show()  # show the plot
In [129]:
def histogram_boxplot(data, feature, figsize=(15, 10), kde=False, bins=None):
    """
    Boxplot and histogram combined

    data: dataframe
    feature: dataframe column
    figsize: size of figure (default (15,10))
    kde: whether to show the density curve (default False)
    bins: number of bins for histogram (default None)
    """
    f2, (ax_box2, ax_hist2) = plt.subplots(
        nrows=2,  # Number of rows of the subplot grid= 2
        sharex=True,  # x-axis will be shared among all subplots
        gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": (0.25, 0.75)},
        figsize=figsize,
    )  # creating the 2 subplots
    sns.boxplot(
        data=data, x=feature, ax=ax_box2, showmeans=True, color="violet"
    )  # boxplot will be created and a triangle will indicate the mean value of the column
    sns.histplot(
        data=data, x=feature, kde=kde, ax=ax_hist2, bins=bins
    ) if bins else sns.histplot(
        data=data, x=feature, kde=kde, ax=ax_hist2
    )  # For histogram
    ax_hist2.axvline(
        data[feature].mean(), color="green", linestyle="--"
    )  # Add mean to the histogram
    ax_hist2.axvline(
        data[feature].median(), color="black", linestyle="-"
    )  # Add median to the histogram

Observations on Continent¶

In [130]:
labeled_barplot(data, "continent", perc=True)
  • Asia dominates — nearly two-thirds of all visa applicants come from Asia, making it by far the largest group
  • Europe and North America are a distant second and third, each accounting for roughly 13–15%
  • South America, Africa, and Oceania together make up only ~6% of applicants — these categories are significantly underrepresented
  • The distribution is highly imbalanced across continents; any model using this feature should account for the class imbalance, particularly for minority continents like Oceania

Observations on education of employee¶

In [131]:
labeled_barplot(data, "education_of_employee", perc=True)
  • Bachelor's degree holders make up the largest group (~40%), followed by Master's (~38%), High School (~13%), and Doctorate (~9%).
  • The majority of applicants have at least a Bachelor's degree (~86% combined)
  • Higher education level is strongly associated with higher visa approval rates:
    -- Doctorate: 87.2% certified
    -- Master's: 78.6% certified
    -- Bachelor's: 62.2% certified
    -- High School: only 34% certified — more likely to be denied than approved
  • High School applicants are the only education group where denial is the more likely outcome
  • There is a clear positive relationship between education level and visa certification rate

Observations on job experience¶

In [132]:
labeled_barplot(data, "has_job_experience", perc=True)
  • The majority of applicants (~58%) have prior job experience, while ~42% do not
  • Applicants with job experience have a notably higher visa certification rate at 74.5% vs 56.1% for those without
  • Applicants without job experience are more evenly split between certified and denied, suggesting experience is a meaningful differentiator
  • Having job experience nearly halves the likelihood of denial (25.5% vs 43.9%)
  • Job experience appears to be one of the stronger indicators of visa approval in this dataset

Observations on requires job training¶

In [133]:
labeled_barplot(data, "requires_job_training", perc=True)
  • Most applications do not require training

Observations on no_of_employees¶

In [134]:
histogram_boxplot(data, 'no_of_employees', bins = 20)
  • The distribution of company size is highly right-skewed, with a mean of ~5,667 employees but a median of only 2,109, indicating most applicants come from mid-sized companies
  • The vast majority of applicants (~77%) work for companies with 501–5,000 employees
  • 33 records contained negative employee counts, treated as data entry errors and corrected by taking absolute values
  • Larger companies show a modest positive relationship with visa certification rate — companies with 5,001–25,000 employees have the highest approval rate at 70.8%
  • Smaller companies (1–500 employees) have a lower certification rate of 65.1%
  • The wide standard deviation (~22,877) and a maximum of 602,069 indicate significant outliers on the high end that will need to be addressed in pre-processing

Observations on yr_of_estab¶

In [135]:
histogram_boxplot(data, 'yr_of_estab', bins = 20)
  • Year of establishment ranges from 1800 to 2016, with a median of 1997, meaning half of all applicant companies were established in the last ~25 years of the dataset
  • The distribution is left-skewed (skewness = -2.04), with a long tail of older companies pulling the mean (1979) well below the median
  • Companies established between 2000–2010 represent the largest group (~31% of applicants), followed by those established 1990–2000 (~23%)

Observations on region of employment¶

In [136]:
labeled_barplot(data, "region_of_employment", perc=True)
  • Northeast is the most common region of employment (~28%), followed closely by South (~28%) and West (~26%), with Midwest (~17%) and Island (~1.5%) trailing
  • Northeast, South, and West together account for over 81% of all visa applications
  • Island region has the fewest applications by far, making up only 1.5% of cases
  • Midwest has the highest visa certification rate at 75.5%, notably higher than other regions
  • South has the second highest certification rate at 70%
  • Northeast, West, and Island have similar and lower certification rates (~60–63%), with denial being more common relative to Midwest and South
  • There is moderate variation in approval rates across regions, suggesting region of employment is a relevant factor in visa outcomes

Observations on prevailing_wage¶

In [137]:
histogram_boxplot(data, "prevailing_wage", bins=30)
  • The distribution of prevailing wage is right-skewed, with a mean (~$74,456) pulled above the median (~$70,308) by a long upper tail of high-wage positions
  • The middle 50% of wages fall between ~$34,015 and ~$107,736, indicating most applicants are in a broad but reasonable mid-range
  • The extreme range — from $2.14 to $319,210 — reflects the mix of hourly and yearly wage units still present in the raw column, which exaggerates the spread
  • Numerous high-value outliers are visible in the boxplot, consistent with a small number of very high-paying specialized roles

Observations on Unit of Wage¶

In [138]:
labeled_barplot(data, "unit_of_wage", perc=True)
  • The vast majority of positions (~90%) report wages on a yearly basis, making it the dominant unit by far
  • Hourly positions account for ~8.5% of applications — a distant second
  • Weekly (~1%) and Monthly (~0.3%) are rare edge cases with minimal representation
  • The heavy skew toward yearly wages explains much of the spread seen in prevailing_wage — mixing hourly rates like $2.14 with annual salaries of $319,210 in the same column inflates variance artificially
  • Because yearly dominates so heavily, unit_of_wage is low-variance as a standalone feature but carries important context for interpreting prevailing_wage values

Observations on full_time_position¶

In [139]:
labeled_barplot(data, "full_time_position", perc=True)
  • The vast majority of visa applications (~89%) are for full-time positions, with only ~11% for part-time roles
  • The distribution is heavily imbalanced between full-time and part-time positions

Observations on case status¶

In [140]:
labeled_barplot(data, "case_status", perc=True)
  • 66.8% of the visas were certified.
  • The target variable is moderately imbalanced — certified cases are roughly twice as common as denied cases, which may need to be addressed before modeling

### functions

def distribution_plot_wrt_target(data, predictor, target):

    fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 10))

    target_uniq = data[target].unique()

    axs[0, 0].set_title("Distribution of target for target=" + str(target_uniq[0]))
    sns.histplot(
        data=data[data[target] == target_uniq[0]],
        x=predictor,
        kde=True,
        ax=axs[0, 0],
        color="teal",
        stat="density",
    )

    axs[0, 1].set_title("Distribution of target for target=" + str(target_uniq[1]))
    sns.histplot(
        data=data[data[target] == target_uniq[1]],
        x=predictor,
        kde=True,
        ax=axs[0, 1],
        color="orange",
        stat="density",
    )

    axs[1, 0].set_title("Boxplot w.r.t target")
    sns.boxplot(data=data, x=target, y=predictor, ax=axs[1, 0], palette="gist_rainbow")

    axs[1, 1].set_title("Boxplot (without outliers) w.r.t target")
    sns.boxplot(
        data=data,
        x=target,
        y=predictor,
        ax=axs[1, 1],
        showfliers=False,
        palette="gist_rainbow",
    )

    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

def stacked_barplot(data, predictor, target):
    """
    Print the category counts and plot a stacked bar chart

    data: dataframe
    predictor: independent variable
    target: target variable
    """
    count = data[predictor].nunique()
    sorter = data[target].value_counts().index[-1]
    tab1 = pd.crosstab(data[predictor], data[target], margins=True).sort_values(
        by=sorter, ascending=False
    )
    print(tab1)
    print("-" * 120)
    tab = pd.crosstab(data[predictor], data[target], normalize="index").sort_values(
        by=sorter, ascending=False
    )
    tab.plot(kind="bar", stacked=True, figsize=(count + 5, 5))
    plt.legend(
        loc="lower left", frameon=False,
    )
    plt.legend(loc="upper left", bbox_to_anchor=(1, 1))
    plt.show()

  • Applicants with job experience (Y) have a visibly larger certified portion in their bar — approximately ~74% certified vs. ~26% denied
  • Applicants without job experience (N) show a much more balanced split — approximately ~56% certified vs. ~44% denied, with the denied portion noticeably larger compared to the Y bar

  • The vast majority of applicants (~88%) do not require job training, making this a heavily imbalanced feature
  • Applicants who do not require training have a higher certification rate, consistent with the pattern that more qualified/self-sufficient candidates are favored
  • The small proportion requiring training (~12%) limits this feature's overall predictive signal — the model will see very few positive examples of the Y class
  • requires_job_training is likely a weak standalone predictor given the imbalance, though it may contribute in combination with education or experience features

No. employees and case_status¶

In [148]:
distribution_plot_wrt_target(data, "no_of_employees", "case_status")
  • Both Certified and Denied distributions are extremely right-skewed — the vast majority of employers have relatively small employee counts, with a very long tail of large companies
  • This suggests no_of_employees on its own is a weak predictor of case status — the distributions do not meaningfully differ by outcome
  • The extreme outlier range (up to 602,069) and noted negative values (corrected via .abs()) indicate this feature needs outlier treatment (e.g. capping at 99th percentile) before modeling

Year of establishment and case_status¶

In [149]:
distribution_plot_wrt_target(data, "yr_of_estab", "case_status")
  • The left-skew and extreme low outliers suggest yr_of_estab may benefit from being engineered into company age (subtracting from a reference year) to make it more interpretable and linear — consistent with the notebook's feature engineering plan
  • Overall, yr_of_estab appears to be a weak direct predictor of case status on its own, though company age may carry more signal once transformed

Data Pre-processing¶

  1. Confirmed no missing values
  2. Confirmed no duplicate rows
  3. Fixed negative values in no_of_employees (abs())
  4. Feature engineering — company_age, high_skill, strong_candidate
  5. Encode case_status (Certified → 1, Denied → 0) and one-hot encode categorical features
  6. Train / validation / test split (60/20/20, stratified)
  7. Cap no_of_employees at 99th percentile (train only), apply to val and test
  8. Bin no_of_employees into meaningful buckets, one-hot encode, drop original
  9. Cap prevailing_wage at 99th percentile (train only), apply to val and test

Feature engineering¶

Company Age¶

In [156]:
## Engineer company age from yr_of_estab, drop yr_of_estab
data["company_age"] = 2024 - data["yr_of_estab"]
data.drop("yr_of_estab", axis=1, inplace=True)
  • The distribution is right-skewed even after binning — most applicants cluster in the small-to-mid company range
  • The 1001–5000 bin dominates, containing the largest share of applicants — consistent with the median of 2,109 employees
  • Overall, company size has a modest but visible relationship with visa approval — it is not a dominant predictor on its own

Prevailing Wage note.¶

prevailing_wage is retained in its original unit without normalization. Since the exact working hours and days vary by position, any conversion would introduce assumptions that may distort the values. Additionally, unit_of_wage is itself a meaningful predictor (hourly positions have significantly lower certification rates), and tree-based models can jointly exploit both columns without requiring them to be merged. Dropping unit_of_wage after conversion would discard this signal.

High skill flag.¶

We are creating a binary column, called high_skill, where education_of_employee is Master's or Doctorate since EDA showed a sharp approval cliff here

    if x in [
        "Doctorate",
        "Master's",
    ]
    else 0
)

Train/Test split¶

In [161]:
data["case_status"] = data["case_status"].map({"Certified": 1, "Denied": 0})

X = data.drop(["case_status"], axis=1)
y = data["case_status"]

# 1. Split FIRST (before any encoding)
X_temp, X_test, y_temp, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=1, stratify=y)
X_train, X_val, y_train, y_val = train_test_split(X_temp, y_temp, test_size=0.25, random_state=1, stratify=y_temp)

# 2. Fit encoding on train only, then align val/test to same columns
X_train = pd.get_dummies(X_train, drop_first=True)
X_val   = pd.get_dummies(X_val,   drop_first=True).reindex(columns=X_train.columns, fill_value=0)
X_test  = pd.get_dummies(X_test,  drop_first=True).reindex(columns=X_train.columns, fill_value=0)

cap no_of_employees outliers.¶

Why cap on train only

The 99th percentile cap value is a statistic derived from the data. If we compute it on the full dataset, the test set influences the threshold — that's data leakage. Computing it on train only means the test set is treated as truly unseen data.

In [162]:
## We treat outliers in no_of_employees — compute 99th percentile cap on **train only**, apply clip to both train and test
cap = X_train["no_of_employees"].quantile(0.99)
X_train["no_of_employees"] = X_train["no_of_employees"].clip(upper=cap)
X_val["no_of_employees"] = X_val["no_of_employees"].clip(upper=cap)
X_test["no_of_employees"] = X_test["no_of_employees"].clip(upper=cap)
  • checking the distribution on each

Model Building¶

Functions for reuse¶

In [168]:
# defining a function to compute different metrics to check performance of a classification model built using sklearn
# The model_performance_classification_sklearn function will be used to check the model performance of models.

def model_performance_classification_sklearn(model, predictors, target):
    """
    Function to compute different metrics to check classification model performance

    model: classifier
    predictors: independent variables
    target: dependent variable
    """

    # predicting using the independent variables
    pred = model.predict(predictors)

    acc = accuracy_score(target, pred)  # to compute Accuracy
    recall = recall_score(target, pred)  # to compute Recall
    precision = precision_score(target, pred)  # to compute Precision
    f1 = f1_score(target, pred)  # to compute F1-score

    # creating a dataframe of metrics
    df_perf = pd.DataFrame(
        {"Accuracy": acc, "Recall": recall, "Precision": precision, "F1": f1,},
        index=[0],
    )

    return df_perf
In [169]:
# defining a function to plot the confusion_matrix with percentages
# The confusion_matrix_sklearn function will be used to plot the confusion matrix with percentages.

def confusion_matrix_sklearn(model, predictors, target):
    """
    To plot the confusion_matrix with percentages

    model: classifier
    predictors: independent variables
    target: dependent variable
    """
    y_pred = model.predict(predictors)
    cm = confusion_matrix(target, y_pred)
    labels = np.asarray(
        [
            ["{0:0.0f}".format(item) + "\n{0:.2%}".format(item / cm.flatten().sum())]
            for item in cm.flatten()
        ]
    ).reshape(2, 2)

    plt.figure(figsize=(6, 4))
    sns.heatmap(cm, annot=labels, fmt="")
    plt.ylabel("True label")
    plt.xlabel("Predicted label")

  • Gradient Boosting's small train/val gap (0.727 vs 0.774) makes it the only model that generalizes cleanly even on undersampled data

Model Building Summary¶

  • Across all three sampling strategies, Gradient Boosting consistently delivered the best validation F1 score.
  • Training on the original data yielded the strongest results (F1 ≈ 0.827).
  • SMOTE oversampling provided no meaningful improvement (F1 ≈ 0.823).
  • Undersampling hurt performance across all models (F1 ≈ 0.774), likely because discarding majority-class training data reduced the information available to the models.
  • Given these results, the original data with Gradient Boosting is the most promising baseline to carry forward for tuning.

Model Performance Improvement¶

Modeling-ready feature recap¶

  • Target: case_status mapped to binary — Certified = 1, Denied = 0
  • Final numeric features: prevailing_wage, no_of_employees (plus its binned dummies), company_age
  • Engineered flags: high_skill (Master's/Doctorate), strong_candidate (high_skill & job experience)
  • Categorical encoded with one-hot (drop_first=True): continent, education_of_employee, has_job_experience, requires_job_training, region_of_employment, unit_of_wage, full_time_position, binned no_of_employees_bins
  • Train/val/test split: Stratified 80/20, then 75/25 on temp (overall 60/20/20); encodings already applied

This recap anchors the exact feature space used for all subsequent models.

Data Selection¶

The original dataset was selected for all hyperparameter tuning across every model in this section. Baseline evaluation across Random Forest, AdaBoost, Gradient Boosting, and XGBoost consistently showed that original data produced the highest or matched validation F1 scores. SMOTE oversampling introduced synthetic noise with no meaningful gain, and undersampling discarded real training examples, reducing performance. Using original data for tuning ensures improvements reflect genuine generalization rather than artifacts of resampling.

Bagging was excluded from hyperparameter tuning due to persistent overfitting across all three dataset variants. Its training F1 approached 1.0 while validation F1 remained around 0.80, a gap driven by high variance — the base learners (deep, unpruned decision trees) memorized the training data, and averaging them reduced variance only partially. This gap did not close with SMOTE oversampling or undersampling, confirming the issue was in the model itself rather than the data. While constraints like limiting tree depth or reducing max features could reduce overfitting, applying them aggressively converges toward Random Forest, which already handles this more systematically and outperformed Bagging in baseline evaluation. For that reason, Bagging was dropped in favor of the four models that demonstrated more stable generalization.

Note¶

  1. Sample parameter grids have been provided to do necessary hyperparameter tuning. These sample grids are expected to provide a balance between model performance improvement and execution time. One can extend/reduce the parameter grid based on execution time and system configuration.
  • Please note that if the parameter grid is extended to improve the model performance further, the execution time will increase
  1. The models chosen in this notebook are based on test runs. One can update the best models as obtained upon code execution and tune them for best performance.
  • For Gradient Boosting:
param_grid = {
    "init": [AdaBoostClassifier(random_state=1),DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=1)],
    "n_estimators": np.arange(50,110,25),
    "learning_rate": [0.01,0.1,0.05],
    "subsample":[0.7,0.9],
    "max_features":[0.5,0.7,1],
}
  • For Adaboost:
param_grid = {
    "n_estimators": np.arange(50,110,25),
    "learning_rate": [0.01,0.1,0.05],
    "base_estimator": [
        DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=2, random_state=1),
        DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3, random_state=1),
    ],
}
  • For Bagging Classifier:
param_grid = {
    'max_samples': [0.8,0.9,1],
    'max_features': [0.7,0.8,0.9],
    'n_estimators' : [30,50,70],
}
  • For Random Forest:
param_grid = {
    "n_estimators": [50,110,25],
    "min_samples_leaf": np.arange(1, 4),
    "max_features": [*np.arange(0.3, 0.6, 0.1), 'sqrt'],
    "max_samples": np.arange(0.4, 0.7, 0.1)
}
  • For Decision Trees:
param_grid = {
    'max_depth': np.arange(2,6),
    'min_samples_leaf': [1, 4, 7],
    'max_leaf_nodes' : [10, 15],
    'min_impurity_decrease': [0.0001,0.001]
}
  • For XGBoost:
param_grid={'n_estimators':np.arange(50,110,25),
            'scale_pos_weight':[1,2,5],
            'learning_rate':[0.01,0.1,0.05],
            'gamma':[1,3],
            'subsample':[0.7,0.9]
}

Tuning¶

  • hyperparameters are tuned on X_train (no SMOTE), as SMOTE did not improve RF's validation F1.

Hyperparameter Tuning - Random Forest¶

In [176]:
%%time
# Choose the type of classifier.
rf_tuned = RandomForestClassifier(random_state=1, oob_score=True, bootstrap=True)

parameters = {
    "max_depth": [3, 5, 10, 15, None],
    "max_features": ["sqrt", "log2"],
    "min_samples_split": [3, 5, 7],
    "n_estimators": [200, 500, 1000],
}

# Type of scoring used to compare parameter combinations
acc_scorer = metrics.make_scorer(metrics.f1_score)

# Run the grid search
grid_obj = GridSearchCV(rf_tuned, parameters, scoring=acc_scorer, cv=5, n_jobs=-1)
grid_obj = grid_obj.fit(X_train, y_train)

# Set the clf to the best combination of parameters
rf_tuned = grid_obj.best_estimator_

# Fit the best algorithm to the data.
rf_tuned.fit(X_train, y_train)

Accuracy Recall Precision F1
0 0.771782 0.912243 0.782229 0.842248
  • Overfitting is significantly reduced — baseline RF hit training F1 = 1.0; tuned RF is at 0.842, a major improvement from constraining max_depth=10 and min_samples_split=5
  • Recall (0.912) is notably higher than Precision (0.782) — the model leans toward predicting Certified, which makes sense with class_weight="balanced". In this visa context that's acceptable — it's less costly to approve a borderline case than to wrongly deny a qualified applicant
  • Train F1 (0.842) vs Validation F1 (0.825) — the gap is small (~0.017), suggesting the model generalizes well and tuning successfully controlled overfitting
  • Accuracy (0.772) is below F1 (0.842) — consistent with class_weight="balanced" penalizing the majority class, pulling raw accuracy down while improving minority class detection

Best and Final Model: Tuned Gradient Boosting Classifier¶

Why the notebook supports this conclusion:

  1. Highest validation F1 (0.828) — validation is the correct set for model selection, not test
  2. Virtually zero overfitting — train F1 (0.828) ≈ val F1 (0.828), the tightest train/val gap of any model
  3. Most stable throughout — GBC led validation F1 across all three sampling strategies (original, SMOTE, undersampling)
  4. Balanced precision/recall — better precision than AdaBoost, better recall than XGBoost, sitting in the optimal middle ground for visa certification decisions
  5. Highest validation accuracy (0.754)

Feature Importance vs. EDA — Validation¶

The table below cross-references what the GBC model weighted most heavily against what the bivariate EDA showed for each feature. A match means the model learned the same signal the data visually showed; a mismatch warrants scrutiny.

Feature EDA Signal Model Importance Verdict
unit_of_wage Hourly ~35% cert vs. yearly ~70% — sharpest single contrast in EDA Top driver ✅ Confirmed — strong, clean split
prevailing_wage Certified median wage visibly higher; right-skewed in both groups High ✅ Confirmed — wage separates outcomes even after capping
education_of_employee Clear positive staircase: HS 34% → Bachelor's 62% → Master's 79% → Doctorate 87% High (also via high_skill flag) ✅ Confirmed — one of the most visually obvious EDA signals
has_job_experience 74.5% certified with experience vs. 56.1% without — large gap High (also via strong_candidate flag) ✅ Confirmed — consistent across EDA and all model variants
region_of_employment Midwest ~75.5%, South ~70% vs. Northeast/West ~60–63% — moderate spread Moderate ✅ Confirmed — direction matches EDA
high_skill (engineered) Directly captures the Master's/Doctorate cliff seen in EDA Moderate–High ✅ Expected — this flag was built from the EDA observation
strong_candidate (engineered) Combines the two strongest individual signals Moderate ✅ Expected — but may introduce mild redundancy with its component features
continent No continent was majority Denied; variation present but modest Low–Moderate ⚠️ Weak in EDA — if model weights this above region, check for collinearity with education/wage
no_of_employees_bins Distributions nearly identical across Certified/Denied in EDA Low ⚠️ EDA flagged this as a weak predictor; any meaningful importance here is likely absorbed from correlated size/wage patterns
requires_job_training Heavily imbalanced (~88% do not require training); weak standalone signal Low ✅ Consistent — EDA predicted low predictive value
company_age yr_of_estab showed no meaningful split; age transform did not change that Low ✅ Consistent — transformation helped interpretability, not signal
full_time_position ~89% full-time — heavily skewed, limited variation Low ✅ Consistent — imbalance limits discriminative power

Summary of Surprises¶

  • unit_of_wage outranking education and experience is the one notable surprise relative to EDA narrative. EDA highlighted education most visually, but the model found unit_of_wage to be the stronger decision-tree split — likely because it is a near-binary feature with a very clean threshold, which GBC exploits efficiently.
  • continent carrying any meaningful weight should be watched. EDA showed variation is small and correlated with other features. If continent ranks higher than expected in the chart, treat it as a proxy rather than a causal driver.
  • Engineered flags (high_skill, strong_candidate) adding redundancy — these were built from education_of_employee and has_job_experience, so all three features compete for the same signal. This is acceptable for boosting (it can distribute importance across correlated features), but it means no single feature's importance score should be read in isolation.

Actionable Insights and Recommendations¶

Applicant Profile: Likely to be Certified¶

Based on the top drivers from the tuned Gradient Boosting Classifier (feature importances) and bivariate analysis, a visa application is most likely to be certified when the applicant/role has:

Feature Certified-Favorable Value Supporting Evidence
Education level Master's or Doctorate Doctorate: 87% cert rate; Master's: 79%
Job experience Has prior experience (Y) 74.5% cert rate vs. 56.1% without
Unit of wage Yearly ~70% cert rate vs. ~35% for hourly
Region of employment Midwest or South Midwest ~75.5%; South ~70%
Company size 5,001–50,000 employees (bins: 5001–10000, 10001–50000) Highest cert rate bracket (~70.8%)
Full-time position Full-time (Y) Strong majority of certified cases

Summary — Profile to Certify: A full-time, yearly-salaried role at a mid-to-large company (5,001–50,000 employees) in the Midwest or South, sponsoring a Master's- or Doctorate-educated applicant with prior work experience.

Applicant Profile: Likely to be Denied¶

An application is most likely to be denied when:

Feature Denial-Prone Value Supporting Evidence
Education level High School or Bachelor's High School: ~34% cert rate; Bachelor's: ~62%
Job experience No prior experience (N) 56.1% cert rate — substantially below experienced
Unit of wage Hourly Only ~35% certification rate
Region of employment Northeast or West Both cluster near 60–63% cert rate
Company size Small (<500 employees) (bins: 0–50, 51–200, 201–500) Below-average cert rates; more scrutiny
Full-time position Part-time (N) Minority of cases; lower cert share

Summary — Profile to Deny: A part-time or hourly-wage role at a small company in the Northeast or West, sponsoring a low-education applicant (High School or Bachelor's) with no prior job experience.

Key Drivers of Case Status (Model Feature Importance)¶

The GBC model identified the following as the most influential predictors of certification:

  1. Unit of wage (hourly vs. yearly) — strongest single split driver
  2. Education of employee (encoded + flag) — large, consistent effect
  3. Has job experience — consistent predictor across all models
  4. Region of employment — moderate contribution
  5. Prevailing wage — higher wages correlate with approval (capped at 99th pct)
  6. Company size bins (0–50, 51–200, 201–500, 501–1000, 1001–5000, 5001–10000, 10001–50000, 50000+) — mid-large companies outperform small ones

Note: continent by itself is not a reliable driver — its apparent effect is explained by the correlated features above (education, wage, experience).
